title: Use prime factors as the building blocks
chapter: Use prime factors as the building blocks
goal: Worked example: the smallest multiplier that turns 90 into a perfect square.

scenes.visual: Show ninety and a blank multiplier, then a perfect square with an unknown side.
scenes.narration: What is the smallest positive whole number that you can multiply ninety by to make a perfect square? Try to think of ninety as a collection of prime pieces. A square will let those pieces split into two identical groups.

scenes.visual: Arrange the prime tiles of ninety into two rows of potential pairs and reveal which slots are full.
scenes.narration: Ninety factorises into two times three times three times five. Each prime needs an even number of copies in a square. The threes already make a pair. The two and the five each appear once. Put a space for a partner beside each of them.

scenes.visual: Slide one two and one five into the empty places, then collect the additional tiles as a multiplier of ten.
scenes.narration: Supply one more two and one more five. Those are the missing tiles. Their product is ten, so multiplying ninety by ten adds just the two partners we need. Now each prime has an even count.

scenes.visual: Separate the completed rows and connect two products of thirty to the area of a square.
scenes.narration: Ninety times ten is nine hundred. Split its tiles into two identical groups, each with a two, a three and a five. Each group multiplies to thirty. Thirty times thirty is nine hundred, so the new number is a square.

scenes.visual: Use divisibility by two and five to show why the multiplier is at least ten.
scenes.narration: Could a smaller positive multiplier work? Any multiplier that works must supply a two and a five, because those counts start odd. A number divisible by the two distinct primes two and five is a multiple of ten. Ten is the first positive multiple and we have shown it works.

scenes.visual: Display the minimum pairing method, then introduce the notebook problem for sixty.
scenes.narration: For a square, pair every prime. Choose one partner for each prime whose count is odd. Try the same proof with sixty. Find the smallest positive whole number to multiply sixty by to make a square, and check your answer by splitting the new prime tiles into two equal groups.

notebook_exercise: Find the smallest positive whole number that multiplies 60 to make a perfect square.
notebook_answer: 60 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 5, so multiply by 3 x 5 = 15, giving 900.
